chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Hafs ibn Qurt, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever claims that Allah commands evil and immorality has lied against Allah. Whoever claims that good and evil exist without the will of Allah has expelled Allah from His sovereignty. Whoever claims that sins are committed without the power of Allah has lied against Allah. And whoever lies against Allah, Allah will enter him into the Fire.'

key_terms.السُّوء: evil/harm — denotes moral wrongdoing or harmful action
key_terms.الْفَحْشَاء: immorality/indecency — gross indecent acts, often associated with sexual immorality
key_terms.الْمَعَاصِي: sins/disobedience — acts of transgression against divine commands
key_terms.سُلْطَان: sovereignty/authority — absolute dominion and power, specifically divine lordship over creation
key_terms.مَشِيئَة: divine will/desire — the operative will of God that encompasses all that exists and occurs

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet Muhammad say about divine will and human responsibility in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (as) transmits a saying of the Prophet (saww) addressing two extreme theological positions regarding divine agency. The first condemned view is that Allah commands evil (associated with Ash'ari-style fatalism taken to an extreme). The second condemned view is that good and evil occur entirely independently of Allah's will (associated with Mu'tazilite-style denial of divine omnipotence). The third condemned view is that human sins occur without any enabling power granted by Allah. Together, these three condemnations articulate the Shia theological position known as 'the matter between two matters' (al-amr bayna al-amrayn): human beings have real agency and responsibility, but this agency operates within the framework of Allah's sovereign will and enabling power.
